extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, journalists, editors, and policymakers interested in how mass opinion is formed and transmitted
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical criteria for understanding how public opinion is formed, transmitted, and distorted by social structure, media production constraints, language, attention, and psychology. Useful for analyzing news content, audience reception, and propaganda effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set as organizing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The social set is not a mere economic class but resembles a biological clan; membership is connected with marriage and family and the attitudes and desires involved. Within the social set, opinions encounter canons such as Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form which form the set's self-picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for embedded norms and transmitted traditions when analyzing opinions; these tacit canons determine what is admissible and how judgments are administered. Example phrases from text: 'Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form.' Anti-pattern: treating social membership as only economic without these cultural norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social leaders as custodians and foreign-affairs ministry
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain individuals (social leaders, augurs) are recognized custodians and interpreters of a set's social pattern; they must know what preserves integrity of their set and also know what other sets are doing, functioning like a ministry of foreign affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyses, identify local social leaders and gates (who grant invitations, signal arrival/status) and track how their judgments and contacts shape wider opinion. Note their sensitivity to integrity and hierarchical position; they create and enforce channels of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and opportunity shape circulation of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal channels (exceptional people who move between sets) establish flows from one set to another through which imitation and standards circulate; where such channels are absent, mediated accounts (press, moving pictures) serve to develop social hierarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence/absence of cross-set interpersonal channels and the degree to which mediated representations substitute; where direct contact is limited, expect stronger influence of mass media and standardized portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiant points of conventionality and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sets act as 'radiant points of conventionality' that are imitated downward: social superiors are imitated by inferiors; the powerful and cosmopolitan elite have international influence, and at that level public and private affairs merge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing cultural or opinion diffusion, identify which groups serve as models and how their private practices become public norms; consider disproportionate influence of cosmopolitan elites on nationwide opinions and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of time and attention for public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Average individuals give very limited time to informing themselves about public affairs (roughly a quarter of an hour daily in studied groups); time and attention available for not taking opinions for granted are small and easily interrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure practical attention budgets of audiences; short attention spans imply that messages must be concise and that depth of opinion formation will often be shallow. Beware of overestimating citizens' time for complex public matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of attention across news features
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers prioritize particular newspaper features (local news, politics, finance, editorials, foreign news, etc.) in varying proportions; these conscious preferences correspond reasonably to the space editors allocate (historical data show sizable share devoted to public-affairs topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare audience preferences with editorial allocation when evaluating media influence; understand demographic differences (gender, profession) in feature preferences and their implications for content strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are principal but not sole information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: While newspapers are the principal means of reporting the unseen environment, magazines, public forums, churches, meetings, women's clubs, and news serials in moving pictures supplement the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple media channels in analyses of information flow and opinion formation; do not treat newspapers in isolation, especially for populations with different media mixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed, coding, and compression degrade transmitted meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Telegraphy, coding, translation, and editorial culling telescope complex events into short dispatches; messages are coded for wire and reconstituted, often losing nuance and detail in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how production constraints (cost of telegraphy, coding systems, translation, editorial compression) introduce omissions and distortions. Example: compressed cabled dispatches and the culling from long statements to short print items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is an imperfect, variable vehicle of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are not unique names for facts; meanings shift over time and across cultures ('words are tokens'; 'dictionary of faded metaphors'); identical words evoke different images in different readers, and rhetorical richness is lost as speech is standardized and distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious relying on single-word labels; account for semantic drift, cultural differences in connotation, and 'word-exchange' fluctuations. In cross-cultural or mass communication, translate not only words but implied value-currencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited literacy and comprehension reduce effective audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Many in the mass audience can either not read or cannot understand complex prose; even among those who can, only a minority have time to devote attention, so words function mainly as cues for imagined composites rather than full factual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by literacy and comprehension ability. For broad influence, craft messages that account for limited processing capacity and that use robust cues rather than reliance on dense argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping and composite mental images from words
rubrics_metrics.description: Single place- or group-names evoke composite, often stereotyped images (e.g., 'Mexico', 'Japan', 'alien') that substitute for detailed knowledge and guide opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and identify prevailing stereotypes when evaluating public reactions; corrective strategies require supplying alternative salient images or richer factual cues rather than abstract rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity and discrimination as essential intellectual qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences, and appreciate variety (lucidity of mind) is crucial for sound public opinion; such discriminations vary widely across individuals and groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the quality of public discourse or designing educational interventions, prioritize measures that foster discriminative skills: critical thinking training, exposure to contrasting examples, and opportunities for focused reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatigue, distraction, and urban environment flatten discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: External conditions — noise, odor, heat, crowdedness, incessant stimuli of city life, and monotony of routine work — reduce attention quality, flatten associative responses, and impair the ability to discern differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for environmental context of information consumption (commuting, factories, crowded homes). Policies or media strategies that assume quiet reflective attention will overestimate audience capacity in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional conflicts and unconscious complexes distort cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional conflicts, personal animosities, class feeling, racial prejudice, ambition, and other unconscious constellations of feeling intermittently distort reading, thinking, talking and behavior — measurable in slowed or aberrant associative responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that cognitive responses are not purely rational; factor in likely emotional distorters when predicting reception and persistence of opinions. Empirical tests of association speed/quality reveal these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience susceptibility varies — broad vs narrow appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'broad appeal' targets susceptibilities widely distributed across the population, while a 'narrow' appeal targets uncommon susceptibilities; the same individual may respond differently at different 'psychic levels' or times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment messaging by psychic level and susceptibility. For mass mobilization favor broad cues (e.g., visually salient, emotionally resonant), while specialist persuasion should target narrower, higher-discrimination audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple refractors of the unseen environment produce distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship and privacy at the source, physical and social barriers, scanty attention, poverty of language, distraction, unconscious feelings, wear-and-tear and other limitations combine to thwart clarity and justice of perception, substitute misleading fictions for workable ideas, and remove checks on deliberate misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating information quality and public opinion robustness, identify and enumerate these refracting factors; mitigation requires improving source transparency, reducing transmission censorship, enriching language/cues, and increasing audience attention and stamina.
